# Corpus Mining: Richard Rutt, *The Book of Changes (Zhouyi): A Bronze Age Document*

**Source PDF**: `/mnt/agents/upload/the-book-of-changes-zhouyi-a-bronze-age-document-0700704671_compress.pdf` (514 pp PDF; book = Routledge, Durham East-Asia Series No. 1, 1996/2002; ISBN 0-7007-0467-1)
**Author**: Richard Rutt (1925–2011), sinologist, Bishop of Leicester; translation draws on Kunst (1985 PhD "kit of tools"), Shaughnessy, Li Jingchi, Gao Heng, Zhang Zhenglang.
**Status**: The single most important book of the three — a scholarly recovery of the **oldest textual stratum**: the Zhouyi core text (tags + hexagram statements + line statements) as a Western Zhou diviner's manual, stripped of Ten Wings / Confucian / yin-yang accretions.

> "Chinese sinologists have shown that the book is really a Bronze Age diviner's manual dealing with war and human sacrifice, giving advice to rulers at the dawn of literature." — Preface (p. ix)

---

## 1. STRATA OF THE TEXT (the grammatical layers)

Rutt's stratification (dates are his):

| Stratum | Content | Date (Rutt) | Evidence/pages |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S0 — Pre-textual numerals** | "Bagua numerals" (bagua shuzi fuhao): groups of 6 numerals (1–9) inscribed at end of oracle-bone, bronze, ceramic inscriptions | oldest reliably dated from reign of **Wuding c. 1238–1180 BC** (Shang) into early Western Zhou | pp. 98–100 |
| **S1 — Oracles (zhaoci/shici)** | omen-utterances; proverbs, weather, animal behavior, stars, historical events | oral history "going back three to five centuries or more" before compilation | p. 33; structure pp. 131–2 |
| **S2 — Indications + Observations** | "earliest commentaries on the oracles, dating from a time before moralizing or philosophizing had entered" | added "when the sense of the oracles began to be forgotten" | p. 134 |
| **S3 — Prognostics (duanci)** | valuation words; "probably came last. They are known to have been unstable in Han times" | late additions to line statements | p. 134 |
| **S4 — Compiled Zhouyi** | redaction of tags + hexagram statements + 386 line statements | **"late Western Zhou times, possibly the last quarter of the ninth century BC (825–800 BC)"** | p. 33 |
| **S5 — Line numbers (chu/2/3/4/5/shang + 6/9)** | "generally believed to have been inserted late in the time of the Warring States"; absent from Shuanggudui slips, present in Mawangdui | Warring States → Han | pp. 129–30 |
| **S6 — Zuo Commentary / Guoyu practice layer** | 19 divination stories, 671–487 BC; earliest descriptions of use | Spring–Autumn | pp. 173–5 |
| **S7 — Ten Wings** | commentarial wings; "Probably none of the Wings was written much before 200 BC, while the last two [Xugua, Zagua] may have been written as late as the early second century AD"; traditionally attributed to Confucius "without good historical or textual cause" | c. 250 BC – AD 100+ | p. 365 |
| **S8 — Han canonization** | "Zhouyi" becomes "Yijing"; stone tablets AD 175–183; received (King Wen) order first attested on these tablets | Han | pp. 38–9, 101 |
| **S9 — Song systematization** | changeable-line theory explicit only in Ouyang Xiu (11th c.); Zhu Xi's Yixue qimeng (1186) fixes wand method; Fuxi/xiantian binary order "probably a creation of the Song period" | Song | pp. 154, 160, 440 |

**Composition hypothesis (Rutt's "most probable" reconstruction, p. 134):**
> "in the first place only oracles were collected and later, when the sense of the oracles began to be forgotten, or experience mounted up, the indications and prognostics were added as clues to the significance of the oracles. The prognostics probably came last."

**Hexagram statements (guaci/tuan) are NOT summaries of the line statements** — a load-bearing structural fact:
> "the hexagram statement does not summarize the theme of its line statements, and in most cases has no thematic connection with them." (p. 123)
> "There is no objective evidence" that hexagram statements are older than line statements (p. 125). They are "possibly the most defective section of Zhouyi" (p. 126).

---

## 2. THE BRONZE-AGE SYNTAX — smallest fragment grammar (CORE FINDING)

### 2.1 The four-slot line-statement grammar (pp. 131–134)

Each **line statement (yaoci)** is a conglomerate of up to four formulaic elements. Chinese names from Li Jingchi, *Zhouyi tanyuan* (1978):

| Slot | Chinese term (Rutt's rendering) | Definition | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **shici** — ORACLE | "the heart of the line statement, a phrase or sentence that encapsulates the divinatory value of each line... proverbs... weather conditions, accidents, the behaviour of birds or animals, the appearance of stars, the condition of buildings or natural features... or significant historical events" (p. 132) | omen-image |
| 2 | **gaoci** — INDICATION | "indicative in the predictive sense... indicate the effect and value of the oracle, frequently defining the type of problem (choosing a house site, choosing a bride, expecting an attack, planning a military expedition, etc)" (p. 132) | domain/action scope |
| 3 | **duanci** — PROGNOSTIC | one of four standard words: **ji, li, jiu, xiong**; "syntactically absolute" (pp. 132–3) | valuation |
| 4 | **yanci** — OBSERVATION | "elaborates or comments on the prognostic, sometimes suggesting a degree of modification, even contradiction"; typically contains **hui** 'trouble' or **lin** 'distress' (Shaughnessy 1983, from oracle-bone studies) (pp. 133–4) | temporal modulation / hedging |

- "Most lines have two or three elements, and some have one element only. Any of the four may be lacking, even the oracle. (Seven lines now have no oracle: 6:5, 25:4, 34:2, 40:base, 45:2, 45:4 and 57:5.)" (p. 131)
- Total line statements: **386** (64×6 + 2 supernumerary). Length per hexagram's line set: 26 chars (Hex 56) to 84 (Hex 47), average 54 (p. 129).
- Slot order is not fixed: "The oracle does not always precede the indications and observations." (p. 221)

### 2.2 Valuation-term inventory (the prognostic/observation morphemes) — pp. 133–4

| Term | Gloss (Rutt) | Frequency | Properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ji** 吉 | 'auspicious' | **147×** — "the commonest word of independent meaning in Zhouyi" | never negated; qualified as yuanji 'most auspicious' (12×), zhongji 'ultimately auspicious' (10×); the only standard prognostic common in oracle-bone inscriptions |
| **li** 危/厲 | 'dangerous' (originally 'scorpion') | 27× | "a threat of failure or trouble... if matters are handled with circumspection, the dangers... may be avoided" |
| **jiu** 咎 | 'misfortune' | 100×, but **93× negated as wujiu** 無咎 'no misfortune' | "'No misfortune'... is effectively the second most favourable prediction"; variants: wu dajiu, feijiu, he jiu, he qi jiu |
| **xiong** 凶 | 'disastrous' | 88× | worst prognostic; never negated; once zhongxiong 'ultimately disastrous'; etymology "malevolent astral influences" |
| **ta** 他 | 'unexpected calamity' | 3× (8:base, 28:4, 61:base) | rarer, "not in the same class as the four major prognostics" |
| **hui** 悔 | 'trouble' | 34×, of which **19× are hui wang** 悔亡 'troubles disappear' | subsidiary prognostic in observations; objective (events), NOT later subjective 'regret': "Bronze Age realpolitik had little room for indulgence in remorse" |
| **lin** 吝 | 'distress' | 20×, never negated; 2× xiao lin 'little distress' (21:3, 45:3) | "not as bad as jiu and xiong" |

Note also: the commonest word of all in Zhouyi is the negative particle **wu** (p. 133).

### 2.3 The "four qualities" — yuan heng li zhen as formulaic morphemes (pp. 126–8)

- **NOT originally a fourfold formula**: "The concatenation yuanheng lizhen occurs only six times." One or more of the four occur in **50 of 64 hexagram statements**. (p. 126)
- Correct decomposition: **two items, yuanheng and lizhen**. "'Grand sacrifice' and 'Propitious prognostication' seem to be what they originally meant" (p. 128).
- Grammatically "yuan and li are modifiers, heng and zhen are substantives or verbs" (p. 127).
- **zhen** = the core prognostication verb/noun: 'augury' / 'to divine'; with >100 occurrences each, li and zhen "are among the ten commonest words in Zhouyi" (p. 127).
- Competing scholarly glosses recorded:
  - Rutt: yuanheng = 'Supreme offering' (heng alone = 'Offering'); lizhen = 'Divination favourable'.
  - Shaughnessy: yuanheng = **'primary receipt'**, lizhen = **'beneficial to divine'** — theory: casting happened in stages; yuanheng lizhen meant the first augury was "received by the spirits and a further casting of lots was recommended" (p. 128).
  - Kunst: "Grand treat. Favourable determination." (p. 128)
- In line statements, yuan occurs only in **yuanji** 'most auspicious'; heng 7× (4× absolute, 3× = 'offering sacrifice').
- Later moralization: by Ten Wings times the four became **si de** 'four virtues' = sublimity / accomplishment / furtherance / perseverance (Wenyan, Zuozhuan Mu Jiang story, pp. 126, 187, 435).

### 2.4 Formulaic INDICATION phrases (recurring slots) — p. 123

> "'Favourable for crossing a big river' (7 times); 'Favourable when there is somewhere to go' (6 times); 'Favourable for meeting great men' (4 times); and many others used much less frequently."

These are the bronze-age "action-domain" templates: fording rivers, travel, audiences, marriage, military expeditions, sacrifices, lawsuits, illness, captives.

### 2.5 Language register (pp. 205–6)

- "Early Old Chinese": verbs have no voice/person/tense/mood; nouns no number/case; no punctuation; parataxis ("the grammar of telegrams"); "practically no grammatical expression of the conditional" — only **nai** and **ze** ('then/and') mark sequence.
- Maspero: "language which is concise to the point of obscurity, crammed with technical terms and with short little phrases having no connection between them" (p. 205).
- Nearest parallels: oracle-bone notes and fragments of popular songs; many line statements **rhyme** (Rutt prints rhyming translations deliberately).
- **Prognostications were often delivered in extempore gnomic verse** (Zuo Commentary rhymes are diviners' words, not lost text) (pp. 172–3).

## 3. SMALLEST FRAGMENTS — inventory

### 3.1 Pre-figural primitives: the bagua numerals (pp. 98–100) — PRE-YIN/YANG-LINE EVIDENCE

- Groups of six-part symbols on Shang/early-Western-Zhou oracle bones, bronzes, ceramics; identified as proto-hexagrams by Zhang Zhenglang (1978 conference).
- "When the signs are numerals, they are easily recognized Chinese figures from 1 to 9, in groups such as **766718**" (p. 100). Transcription rule: **odd numbers → whole lines, even numbers → broken lines**.
- Six signs occur "sometimes as two groups of three chevrons placed side by side, most often as a group of six lines, chevrons, or numerals set vertically one above another" (p. 100). Broken lines "may have three parts, rather than two."
- **Groups of three numerals are later** → "favouring the thesis that **hexagrams are older than trigrams**" (p. 100).
- CRITICAL ANOMALY: "some groups of six figures cannot be obtained by the divination procedures now known, which give only the four numbers 6, 7, 8 and 9. If they were received by counting yarrow-wands, **a method of counting now unknown to us** must have been used" (p. 100).
- "Zhouyi itself shows no consciousness of trigrams, and the six oracles never fall thematically into two sets of three." (p. 98) — the trigram is a later analytic overlay.
- Possible origin of the 6-line form: late-Shang ten-day week shell auguries "inscribed on oracle bones in columns containing six items, often read from bottom to top" (p. 102) [uncertain — Rutt flags as speculation].
- Pentagram (5-line) theory (Barde, Maspero) exists but bagua numeral evidence is "inconclusive" (pp. 96–8, 100).

### 3.2 The line itself

- Two forms: whole (—) and broken (- -). Positionally ordered, built **bottom to top**: "in divining, a hexagram is built up line by line from the bottom as the numbers are received from the yarrow wand counts; and the meaning of the oracles moves from a beginning or base in the bottom oracle to an ending and peak at the top." (pp. 128–9)
- Two states (a later formalization): stable / changeable. Changeable = denoted **zhi** 之: "A zhi B" = "the line of Hexagram A that when changed produces Hexagram B" — originally likely a **genitive particle**, not 'moving to' (pp. 154–5). Line-citation without numbers!
- Changeable lines: "There is nothing either explicit or implicit in Zhouyi to suggest that 'changeable lines' were known in Western Zhou" (p. 154); not in Ten Wings, Wang Bi, or Kong Yingda; explicit in Ouyang Xiu (11th c. AD).
- 6/9 numbering: 9 = whole, 6 = broken; 7 = stable whole, 8 = stable broken. Four line-kinds with shorthand: jiao 'crossed' X (changeable broken), dan 'single' (stable whole), zhe 'broken' (stable broken), chong 'double' O (changeable whole) (p. 156).

### 3.3 The tag (guaming) — the hexagram's name-word

- "In Chinese the hexagrams have never been numbered. They are simply labelled with the tag characters" (p. 101).
- Tags are obscure; in 59/64 hexagrams the tag character appears somewhere in the line statements; only in 15 is it the unifying concept of all six lines; sometimes chosen for its **rhyme** with the line statements (p. 119).
- Rutt's tag glosses (the omen-image vocabulary of the tags), from the translation key (p. 223 area):
  1 qian/active · 2 kun/earth · 3 zhun/massed · 4 meng/dodder · 5 xu/waiting · 6 song/dispute · 7 shi/troops · 8 bi/joining · 9 xiaochu/farming: minor · 10 lü/stepping · 11 tai/great · 12 pi/bad · 13 tongren/mustering · 14 dayou/large, there [is] · 15 qian/rat · 16 yu/elephant · 17 sui/pursuit · 18 gu/mildew · 19 lin/keening · 20 guan/observing · 21 shike/biting · 22 bi/bedight · 23 bo/flaying · 24 fu/returning · 25 wuwang/unexpected · 26 dachu/farming: major · 27 yi/molars · 28 daguo/passing: major · 29 kan/pit · 30 li/oriole · 31 xian/chopping · 32 heng/fixing · 33 dun/– · 34 dazhuang/– · 35 jin/advancing · 36 mingyi/crying pheasant · 37 jiaren/household · 38 kui/espy · 39 jian/stumbling · 40 jie/unloosing · 41 sun/diminishing · 42 yi/enriching · 43 jue(guai)/skipping · 44 gou/locking · 45 cui/together · 46 sheng/going up · 47 kun/beset · 48 jing/well · 49 ge/leather · 50 ding/tripod bowl · 51 zhen/thunder · 52 gen/cleaving · 53 jian/settling · 54 guimei/marriage · 55 feng/thick · 56 lü/sojourner · 57 xun/food offerings · 58 yue(dui)/satisfaction · 59 huan/gushing · 60 jie/juncture · 61 zhongfu/trying captives · 62 xiaoguo/passing: minor · 63 jiji/already across · 64 weiji/not yet across.
  (Note: many tags are concrete omen-things — rat, elephant, pheasant, oriole, pit, well, tripod, leather, mildew, dodder — not abstractions. Rutt deliberately rejects the moralized renderings: e.g. 15 = 'rat' where Wilhelm has 'Modesty', 16 = 'elephant' where Wilhelm has 'Enthusiasm'.)

### 3.4 Omen-image vocabulary in the oracles (from the translation, pp. 224–287)

Recurring image classes:
- **Celestial/astronomical**: the Dragon stars (Hex 1 dragon series keyed to heliacal risings of the Dragon constellation: "Around 800 BC in midwinter at dusk the Dragon stars were all invisible below the horizon" — Translation note 1:base, p. 291); midday (55); stars.
- **Animals**: dragons (submerged, in fields, leaping, flying, soaring, headless flock, fighting — Hex 1 & 2); mares (2:statement "Favourable augury for mares"); tiger's tail (10); fox (64 "not yet across" — fox crossing ice); pig-fish (61 [possibly 'dolphin', uncertain]); pheasant (36); oriole (30); rat (15); elephant (16); birds generally (62 "bird's message"); horses of Marquis Kang (35); cows (30).
- **Plants/agriculture**: dodder (4), crops, "farming minor/major" (9/26), melons, withered willow/poplar (28).
- **Built/crafted things**: well (48 — full oracle series: muddy well, leaking well, cleaned well, lined well, cold-spring well), tripod/cauldron (50 — "the line means the same as a sacrificial cooking-pot being knocked over" p. 132), cart, belt of rank, robe, jade baton, sacks of grain, bronze arrow, shackles and fetters, aprons and leggings.
- **Landscape/weather**: pit/gorge (29), frost → solid ice (2:base), clouds and rain (9), great winds (2:2), thunder (51), mountain cleaving (52), sands, mud, blood, "blood falls as rain" (2:top).
- **Social/ritual acts**: sacrifices of captives (recurrent: "Sacrificing captives. Supreme offering." 5:statement), beheading foes (30:6), interrogating captives (7:5), banquets for the Son of Heaven (14:3), mustering (13), lawsuits (6), marriage/betrothal (31, 53, 54), funerary keening (19), returning (24), sojourning (56).
- **Body**: molars/teeth (27), thighs, blood, "examine teeth" (27:statement).

### 3.5 Worked example of the full slot grammar — Hexagram 1 (p. 224)

```
1 QIAN/active
Hexagram statement:  Supreme offering. Favourable augury.        [= yuanheng lizhen]
Base (9):  A dragon lies beneath the lake. / No action take.     [oracle + indication]
(9) 2:     Lo, on the fields a dragon bides. /
           To meet with great men well betides.                  [oracle + indication ("standard formula", p. 291)]
(9) 3:     A prince is active all day long and after dark still
           stays alert.            DANGEROUS. NO MISFORTUNE.     [oracle + PROGNOSTIC li + PROGNOSTIC wujiu]
(9) 4:     Sometimes it leaps above the tides. NO MISFORTUNE.
(9) 5:     A dragon through the heavens glides. /
           To meet with great men well betides.
Top (9):   A dragon soaring away. There will be trouble.         [oracle + observation hui]
All (9):   See dragons without heads. AUSPICIOUS.                [supernumerary yong line: oracle + ji]
```

### 3.6 Supernumerary fragments (Hex 1 & 2 only) — pp. 130–1

- 7th line statements prefixed **yong** 用 'to use'; Mawangdui MS instead uses **tong** 通 'to pass through/throughout' → both possibly loans for tong 'all', i.e. "**All (9)**" / "**All (6)**" — the oracle to use when all six lines change. Zuo Commentary calls 1's extra line "qi Kun" ('its Hexagram 2'). "These extra line statements probably do not belong to the oldest stratum."

## 4. RULES (divination & transformation grammar)

### 4.1 Casting grammar — Dayan wand-counting (pp. 158–162)

1. **50 wands provided, 49 used** (one removed). Mathematical necessity: "Counting has to arrive at four possible answers (6, 7, 8 and 9), and the method is division by four in order to discover remainders... The only number that will give the desired results (6, 7, 8 or 9) and no others is 49." (p. 159)
2. Divide 49 at random into two heaps; set one wand aside; count out heaps by fours; discard remainders between fingers (the discard = **bian** 'change', later the word for mathematical 'interim result').
3. Four operations per round (divide, set aside, count by fours, reserve discards); **3 rounds ("changes") per line → 18 operations per hexagram**.
4. Outcomes: **6 = old/changeable broken (X), 7 = stable whole, 8 = stable broken, 9 = old/changeable whole (O)**. 36 wands remain for a whole line, 24 for broken (216 and 144 per homogeneous hexagram; 11,520 for all 384 lines).
5. Probabilities (yarrow): one changeable line ≈ **36%**; 1–2 changeable ≈ 66%; none ≈ 18%; ≥3 ≈ 17%; 6 changeable almost never (Table 18, p. 169). Three-coin method (Tang replacement) flattens probabilities (1/8 vs 1/16 for moving lines [uncertain exact ratio — see p. 166f]).

### 4.2 Oracle-selection rules — "Nanjing rules" (Gao Heng circle, 1920s; reconstruction of Spring–Autumn practice, pp. 169–172)

- Sum the six xiang numbers (6/7/8/9), subtract from **55** (= Dayan's sum 1..10); remainder 1–19 maps to a specific line via a fixed table (remainder {1,12,13}→line 1; {2,11,14}→2; {3,10,15}→3; {4,9,16}→4; {5,8,17}→5; {6,7,18,19}→6).
- Reading rules:
  1. All lines stable → **hexagram statement** is the oracle.
  2. All lines changeable → convert; new hexagram statement is the oracle (Hex 1/2: use the 7th "All" statement).
  3. Indicated line changeable → **that line statement** in the base hexagram is the oracle; ignore other changeable lines.
  4. Indicated line stable ("meeting an 8") → hexagram statement(s): <3 changeable → base statement; =3 changeable → both statements together; 4–5 changeable → new hexagram statement.
- Rutt: validity "remains unresolved" (p. 172). Zuo statistics (114 lines: 52% stable/48% changeable) deviate from wand probabilities (75/25) → sample not random, or method differed.

### 4.3 Combination/composition rules observed in the text

- **Pairing rule of the received order**: hexagrams arranged in pairs, second = **inversion** of first, except the 8 non-invertible hexagrams (1/2, 27/28, 29/30, 61/62) which pair by **counter-change** (whole↔broken swap) (pp. 101–3). The pairing "treats the hexagrams as fundamental and ignores the constituent trigrams" (p. 98).
- **Mawangdui order** (168 BC MS): octets grouped by upper trigram; lower trigrams cycle in a family order; totally different from received order (pp. 115–7) — proof that "King Wen order" was not fixed before Han.
- **Thematic agglomeration**: "examples into groups of general omens... towards the agglomeration of omens with similar themes" — oracle collections grew by thematic clustering (p. 136 area) [page ~136; text line 6406].
- **Two-process model of a divination event** (p. 172): (1) "work the oracle" (mechanical wand-count → text), (2) interpret + announce prognostication (professional skill, hedged, often in gnomic rhyme).
- Charge/question topics from divination records: "warfare and sacrifices... various troubles and distresses; dreams; new settlements; choice [of sites]; harvest; calamity (discovering which ancestor's spirit [is angry])" (pp. 30–1, 145 area).
- In Zuo practice: 12 of 16 divinations read a single line statement; 4 read hexagram statements; **constituent trigrams used to explain omens in 12 of 22 stories**, invoking natural-force correspondences (Heaven, Earth, Wind, Thunder, Fire, Mountain, Moving Water, Still Water); family correspondences in only 3 stories; **"no use of Five Element or yin/yang theories, and no evidence of a 'philosophy of change'"** (pp. 174–5).
- Earliest datable **reflective (non-divinatory) citation** of Zhouyi: 603 BC (p. 175); earliest philosophical reading: Cai Mo on Hexagram 34, 509 BC (p. 197).

### 5.1 Table 19 — Significances of the eight trigrams (p. 174; the Zuo-commentary stratum)

| QIAN | KUN | GEN | DUI | KAN | LI | ZHEN | XUN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sky | Earth | Mountain | Still water | Moving water | Fire | Thunder | Wind |
| Father | Mother | 3rd son | 3rd daughter | 2nd son | 2nd daughter | 1st son | 1st daughter |

### 5.2 Shuogua paragraphs 7–10 (pp. 447–8; Warring-States/Han stratum)

- **Temperaments (xingqing)**: Qian strong · Kun compliant · Zhen moving · Xun entering · Kan sinking · Li connecting · Gen stopping · Dui pleasing.
- **Animals**: Qian horse · Kun ox · Zhen dragon · Xun cock · Kan pig · Li pheasant · Gen dog · Dui sheep.
- **Body**: Qian head · Kun stomach · Zhen foot · Xun thigh · Kan ear · Li eye · Gen hand · Dui mouth.
- **Family** (by which line position is single): Zhen eldest son, Xun eldest daughter, Kan middle son, Li middle daughter, Gen youngest son, Dui youngest daughter.
- Extended lists (¶11): Qian = heaven, round, prince, father, jade, bronze, cold, ice, deep red, good/old/slim/skewbald horse, tree fruit; Kun = earth, mother, cloth, cauldron, frugality, evenness, cow and calf, stripes, big chariot, crowds, handle-shaft, black earth; Zhen = thunder, dragons, dark-and-pale, diffusion, highroad, eldest son, vehement decisions, green bamboo shoots/reeds, neighing/white-hind-leg/white-star horses, legumes... (list continues pp. 448–9 for all eight).
- **Trigram sequences**: (1) houtian/King Wen compass order (Zhen E, Xun SE, Li S, Kun SW, Dui W, Qian NW, Kan N, Gen NE) — "Nothing is known of its origin... probably not much older than the Ten Wings"; (2) xiantian/Fuxi binary order — Song creation; (3) family order used in Mawangdui lower-trigram cycle and "popular Chinese magic and good-luck charms" (pp. 440–1).

## 6. CANDIDATE DIMENSION ATTRIBUTION (per fragment class)

Dimensions: **Movement** (vectors/where), **Evolution** (becoming/when), **Being** (state/quality), **Design** (structure/form), **Space** (container/resonance).

| Fragment class | Proposed dimension | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Oracle (shici) — omen image ("dragon beneath the lake", "frost underfoot") | **Being** (encodes an observed state/quality of the world at a moment) | oracles are "weather conditions, accidents, the behaviour of birds or animals" (p. 132) — pure state-snapshots. Secondary: Space, insofar as images are resonant containers keyed to domains. |
| Indication (gaoci) — "Favourable for crossing a big river / somewhere to go / meeting great men" | **Movement** (action-vectors: going, fording, traveling, attacking; where/whither) | the recurrent templates are all directed actions (p. 123). |
| Prognostic (duanci) — ji/li/jiu/xiong | **Being** as *valuation axis* — a 4-point quality scale on the state; note it is a **bipolar gradient** (147 ji vs 88 xiong; li = avoidable bad, wujiu = neutralized bad) | pp. 133–4. Could equally seed an independent "Valuation" dimension [flag for lead]. |
| Observation (yanci) — hui wang 'troubles disappear', 'trouble in the end' | **Evolution** (temporal modulation: how the state unfolds/resolves over time; "an auspicious augury will lead to trouble at a later stage") | p. 134. |
| Line position base→top | **Evolution** (built-in narrative time: "meaning... moves from a beginning or base in the bottom oracle to an ending and peak at the top", pp. 128–9; dragon rises base→top in Hex 1 keyed to seasonal rising of Dragon stars, p. 291) | also a Movement (ascent) reading. |
| Tag (guaming) | **Being** (name/identity of the fragment cluster) — but functionally an index/label, i.e. **Design** | pp. 101, 118–9. |
| Hexagram figure (2^6 combinatorial object; pair rules inversion/counter-change) | **Design** (pure structure/form; Leibniz binary; Mawangdui vs received orderings) | pp. 92–3, 101–117. |
| Bagua numerals (6-digit figures on bones/bronzes) | **Design** — pre-iconic numeric encoding of the same state space; evidence the substrate was *numerical before it was lineal/figural* | pp. 98–100. |
| Casting procedure (49 wands, mod-4, 3 changes) | **Evolution** — the generative operator that produces becoming; bian 'change' = interim result | pp. 158–161. |
| Trigram correspondence overlays (nature/family/body/animals) | **Space** (resonance containers binding hexagram to natural/social/bodily fields) — a *later* addition: Zhouyi "shows no consciousness of trigrams" (p. 98) | pp. 174–5, 447–9. |
| Changeable-line/zhi citation ("A zhi B") | **Movement** (the original vector primitive: one state named by its transformation target, "Hexagram 14 moving to Hexagram 1") | pp. 154–5. |

## 7. LOAD-BEARING QUOTES (book page numbers)

1. "a Bronze Age diviner's manual dealing with war and human sacrifice, giving advice to rulers at the dawn of literature." — Preface, p. ix
2. "the book as we now have it comes from late Western Zhou times, possibly the last quarter of the ninth century BC (825-800 BC); but the material in it may well reflect an oral history going back three to five centuries or more." — p. 33
3. "Each line statement is composed of up to four elements: oracle, indication, prognostic and observation." — p. 131
4. "Ji 'auspicious'... occurs 147 times and is the commonest word of independent meaning in Zhouyi." — p. 133
5. "'Grand sacrifice' and 'Propitious prognostication' seem to be what they originally meant." (on yuanheng / lizhen) — p. 128
6. "The concatenation yuanheng lizhen occurs only six times." — p. 127
7. "Zhouyi itself shows no consciousness of trigrams, and the six oracles never fall thematically into two sets of three." — p. 98
8. "groups such as 766718... Odd numbers are transcribed as whole lines, even numbers as broken lines" — p. 99–100 (Diagram 6)
9. "a method of counting now unknown to us must have been used" (re: numerals outside 6/7/8/9) — p. 100
10. "There is nothing either explicit or implicit in Zhouyi to suggest that 'changeable lines' were known in Western Zhou." — p. 154
11. "A zhi B... 'The line of Hexagram A that when changed produces Hexagram B'" — pp. 154–5
12. "The only number that will give the desired results (6, 7, 8 or 9) and no others is 49." — p. 159
13. "there is no use of Five Element or yin/yang theories, and no evidence of a 'philosophy of change'" (re: Zuo-era practice) — p. 175
14. "in the first place only oracles were collected and later... the indications and prognostics were added as clues... The prognostics probably came last." — p. 134
15. "the hexagram statement does not summarize the theme of its line statements" — p. 123
16. "Yarrow wands are short, tortoise-shells are long" — Zuo Commentary, 656 BC, quoted p. 173
17. "Around 800 BC in midwinter at dusk the Dragon stars were all invisible below the horizon" — Translation note 1:base, p. 291

## 8. UNCERTAINTIES / FLAGS

- [uncertain] Pentagram (5-line) precursor stage: bagua-numeral evidence "inconclusive" (p. 100).
- [uncertain] Whether zhi meant 'moving to' or was a genitive particle — Shaughnessy argued genitive; "completely convincing conclusions cannot be reached" (p. 155).
- [uncertain] Nanjing rules are a 20th-century reconstruction; three formal objections logged (pp. 171–2).
- [uncertain] Six-item bottom-to-top oracle-bone columns as origin of hexagram form — flagged by Rutt as "may have suggested" (p. 102).
- Rutt's tag glosses are deliberately demoralized and sometimes speculative (he stresses all translations are "provisional", Preface p. x).
- The book's own TOC lists "Tags; Hexagram Statements; Line Statements" as the contents of Zhouyi — the tripartite text-unit structure used throughout this file.
